#9450. How ADHD Science Fails Women in Menopause

Menopause worsens ADHD symptoms, but standard assessments do not capture the depth of women’s misery.

Menopause aggravates and elevates ADHD symptoms for a staggering 97.5 percent of women with the condition, according to a survey of 600 women cited in the Journal of Psychiatric Research.1 Complaints include increased difficulty with attention, emotional regulation, and managing everyday demands – symptoms that significantly degrade quality of life yet remain largely unaddressed in midlife ADHD treatment plans.

The Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) – one of the standard measures for assessing common ADHD symptoms – may not fully capture how much menopause interferes with daily life because it was not specifically designed to measure changes in ADHD across hormonal transitions.

While nearly all of the 600 women in the survey reported worsening ADHD symptoms during menopause, their ASRS scores were similar across different hormonal life stages. This apparent contradiction deserves attention. A woman may experience a major change in mental clarity, working memory, motivation, emotional regulation, and managing day-to-day responsibilities without necessarily showing a large change on a standard ADHD symptom checklist.

[Get This Free Download: Menopause and ADHD]

This points to a critical need for better ways to assess ADHD across the lifespan and to understand how hormonal changes may alter its presentation and impact.

Today, we know about ADHD in menopause thanks, largely, to women’s personal accounts. Though surveys and self-reports cannot establish cause and effect in the same way as controlled clinical trials, they are an essential starting point. They can identify patterns and raise questions that researchers need to investigate.

One central question is regarding the safety and efficacy of prescribing hormone replacement therapy (HRT) and/or ADHD medication to women in perimenopause and menopause. Sadly, evidence specifically supporting combined HRT and stimulant treatment remains limited. We need well-designed studies to determine which women might benefit, what treatments are most effective, and how the medications may interact.

[Read: How Hormonal Changes Impact ADHD Symptoms in Women]

The voices of women with ADHD have brought this issue into view. Now clinicians and researchers have an opportunity – and a responsibility – to listen carefully, investigate rigorously, and translate emerging knowledge into better care.

Kathleen Nadeau, Ph.D., is the founder and clinical director of the Institute for Lifespan ADHD Training.

#9449. 16 Ways To Escape The Loneliness Trap And Feel More Connected (P)

From breaking negative thought patterns to finding meaning and connection, these science-backed techniques fight loneliness fast.

Loneliness is an emotion that tells us we do not have enough pleasurable and rewarding social relationships in our lives.

Between 30-40 percent of people around the world report being constantly lonely.

However, psychological research has uncovered a range of simple, sometimes surprising strategies that can ease isolation and help people feel more connected.

From straightforward everyday actions to mindset shifts, here are 16 ways to boost feelings of connection.

#9448. A Parachute for Your ADHD Medication Crash

Most people taking ADHD medication experience an afternoon crash. Here, ADDitude readers reveal effective strategies for a softer landing.

It’s 4 p.m. and your brain is suddenly caught in a riptide. You feel like a swimmer fighting a strong current. The focus, priorities, and momentum that have propelled you forward until now are submerged under a layer of brain fog that rolls in around the same time each day.

This phenomenon is called the ADHD medication crash, and it happens to two-thirds of ADDitude readers who take ADHD medication. When medication levels drop rapidly in the bloodstream, this can result in fatigue, slowed processing speed, and inertia.

According to 3,500 ADDitude survey responses, 57 to 78 percent of stimulant medication users experience a regular crash, with dextroamphetamine and Ritalin LA users reporting the highest prevalence. Even people taking the most popular stimulant medications reported crash prevalence rates of near or above 60 percent. (Users’ experiences with the most popular stimulant medications are shown in the chart below.) The lowest crash prevalence rates were reported by people taking the non-stimulant medications Atomoxetine/Strattera (40%) and guanfacine (52.9%), suggesting that medication crashes are less common with non-stimulant ADHD treatments.

The most common signs of a medication crash, according to ADDitude readers who experience them, include:

The odds of a medication crash increase when an individual is experiencing stress, inadequate sleep, poor diet, and lack of exercise, according to survey respondents. Almost two-thirds of women who experience crashes said their menstrual cycle impacts the crash symptom severity. Readers did not cite medication interactions or caffeine as significant contributors.

The ability to manage household responsibilities is “often” or “always” impaired by medication crashes for 70 percent of survey respondents. Half of crashers say work responsibilities “often” or “always” suffer, and 43 percent say social and family interactions suffer.

#9447. 2 Personality Traits Are Linked to Lower Inflammation

Lower inflammation is associated with less fatigue, a lower risk of depression and a slower decline in reasoning as people age.

Lower inflammation is associated with less fatigue, a lower risk of depression and a slower decline in reasoning as people age.

People who score higher in conscientiousness or extraversion tend to have lower levels of certain markers of inflammation.

Among the qualities that make up conscientiousness, being hardworking and organised stood out.

For extraversion, which includes both sociability and energy, the clearest result was for people who described themselves as active.

These patterns matter because inflammation that stays elevated over time is linked to both physical and psychological health.

Lower levels of long-term inflammation are linked to a lower risk of heart disease, stroke and premature death.

They have also been associated with less fatigue, a lower risk of depression and a slower decline in reasoning as people age.

The researchers pooled data from six studies involving more than 19,000 adults in the United States, England and Japan.

Participants rated how well words such as ‘organised’, ‘hardworking’ and ‘active’ described them.

The researchers then looked at how those answers related to two markers of inflammation in blood samples, C-reactive protein and interleukin-6.

Earlier research had already linked higher conscientiousness with lower levels of both inflammatory markers (Luchetti et al., 2014).

In this study, people who described themselves as organised or hardworking tended to have lower levels of both markers.

Being hardworking showed the strongest association within conscientiousness, even stronger than the association for the overall trait score.

People who scored higher on extraversion tended to have lower C-reactive protein, and much of that association came from how active they said they were.

In fact, being active was more strongly associated with lower C-reactive protein than any other characteristic the researchers examined.

Being talkative showed a small association in the opposite direction, while being lively was associated with lower levels of both inflammatory markers.

In several of the studies, the association with being active held up even after the researchers took other aspects of extraversion into account.

Being active and hardworking may both reflect how much energy people have for everyday tasks.

In earlier research, people who scored higher on the activity aspect of extraversion or the achievement-striving aspect of conscientiousness tended to have better aerobic capacity during a brisk walking test (Terracciano et al., 2013).

Regular physical activity could help explain part of the association with inflammation.

The relationship could run in the other direction, too, if people with higher inflammation feel less energetic and come to see themselves as less active or lively.

The study was published in the journal Psychoneuroendocrinology (Stephan et al., 2026).

#9446. The Urgency of Early ADHD Intervention

Delaying treatment for ADHD until the teen years comes with potential life-long consequences. Here’s what you should know.

Q: I believe my elementary school-age child has ADHD, but my husband doesn’t think so. He refuses to get our child evaluated. I have ADHD and I know this can run in families. What should I do?

This question reflects a dilemma faced by many families: What happens when one parent wants possible signs of ADHD evaluated while another prefers to wait and see? The answer may matter more than many people realize.

Imagine two children entering first grade:

Jacob is bright, curious, and energetic. He struggles to sit still, frequently forgets to turn in his homework, and has difficulty following multi-step instructions. His teacher notices the symptoms and relays these to his parents. Jacob’s pediatrician conducts a comprehensive evaluation and diagnoses Jacob with ADHD.

His parents learn strategies to support him at home. His school implements accommodations. Later, medication becomes part of his treatment plan. Jacob still faces challenges, but he learns how his brain works and develops tools to succeed. He graduates from high school with strong grades and heads off to college.

[Webinar Replay: “6 Principles for Raising a Child with ADHD”]

Now imagine Maya. She is also intelligent, but her suspected ADHD symptoms present differently. She daydreams in class and quietly falls behind. She is emotionally sensitive, often taking criticism to heart and becoming overwhelmed by setbacks that her peers seem to brush off. Her teachers describe her as capable but inconsistent. Because she isn’t disruptive, her struggles are attributed to a lack of effort, disorganization, anxiety, or immaturity.

Year after year, she works harder while feeling increasingly frustrated. As academic demands increase, so do her feelings of self-doubt and inadequacy. By the time she receives an ADHD diagnosis at age 16, her grades have suffered, her confidence has eroded, and she is considering leaving school altogether.

The paths of these two children, one who received early intervention with medication and one who remained untreated until her mid-teens, illustrate a growing concern in ADHD care: It’s not simply about whether children are diagnosed, but when.

[Self-Test: Could Your Preschooler Have ADHD?]

A recent study published in JAMA Psychiatry examined educational outcomes among more than 580,000 individuals with ADHD. The researchers found that children diagnosed earlier in life had significantly better educational outcomes than those diagnosed during adolescence. Earlier diagnosis with associated with higher grade point averages, a greater likelihood of pursuing academic educational tracks, and substantially lower rates of school dropout.

The differences were striking. Individuals diagnosed during the early elementary school years had school dropout rates of approximately 9 percent by age 20, compared with nearly 30 percent among those first diagnosed around age 16. Similar patterns were observed in both males and females. The researchers concluded that adolescents diagnosed later represent a particularly vulnerable group.

The findings do not suggest that a diagnosis alone changes a child’s future. Rather, earlier recognition creates opportunities for intervention. Children identified sooner can access school accommodations, behavioral supports, parent education, and, when appropriate, medication – before years of academic struggles, self-doubt, and declining confidence take hold and begin to shape their identity.

This raises an important question: How many Mayas are sitting in classrooms today, struggling silently while waiting years for recognition or a diagnosis?

Universal ADHD screening offers a potential solution. Many children with ADHD are identified only after academic, social, or emotional difficulties have become impossible to ignore. Screening creates an opportunity to recognize concerns earlier before the consequences of undiagnosed ADHD begin to accumulate. Importantly, screening is not diagnosis. It is simply an invitation to look more closely.

Many critics of universal screening worry about overdiagnosis or unnecessary labeling. Those concerns deserve consideration. However, screening itself does not determine whether a child has ADHD. It merely identifies children who may benefit from a more comprehensive evaluation, meaning that fewer children with significant challenges get overlooked.

Growing evidence suggests that every year of delayed recognition carries educational and emotional costs that are difficult to reverse. Universal screening will not identify every child. But it may help more children find the right path before they wander too far afield.

For many children, the greatest risk may not be receiving an ADHD diagnosis. It may be never receiving one at all.

Here are three actions that caregivers can take:

Greg Mattingly, M.D., is an associate clinical professor at Washington University School of Medicine and co-chair of U.S. Psych Congress.

#9445. Panic attack hangover: 12 ways to recover and feel better

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

You’re finally on the other side of the panic attack. The chest tightness has eased, the shaking has stopped, and your breathing feels more steady. But instead of relief, there’s a strange exhaustion settling in, like you just ran a marathon you don’t remember signing up for. This is often called a panic attack hangover.

The hours (or even days) after a panic episode can feel foggy and disorienting. You might experience headaches, sore muscles, difficulty concentrating, or an overwhelming need to crash. These symptoms can feel alarming if no one ever mentioned they might show up, but they’re actually a normal part of the body’s recovery process.

Understanding what’s happening can ease some of the worry, and having a few gentle tools on hand can make the aftermath feel a little less isolating. Here’s what to know about panic attack hangovers, along with research-backed tips to support yourself through them.

A panic attack hangover is the period of lingering after-effects that follow a panic attack. Even though the rush of fear and physical symptoms has eased, your body can still feel off-balance for hours or even days afterward. Many people describe it as feeling strangely similar to an alcohol hangover: foggy, heavy, and emotionally sensitive.

The experience can be unsettling, especially if you didn’t expect panic to have an “aftermath.” But panic attack hangovers are both common and temporary. They’re simply your body’s way of recovering from an intense stress response.

Note: This guide focuses on panic attacks. If you’ve had an anxiety attack, which builds more gradually, read How to manage symptoms and find ease after an anxiety attack instead.

While panic attack hangovers can happen at any time, the effects aren’t the same for everyone. Still, there are some common symptoms people notice after a panic attack, some more frequently than others.

Fatigue or exhaustion: You might feel like your body’s battery has been completely drained.

Brain fog: You could find it hard to focus, remember things, or think clearly.

Muscle tension or soreness: Your jaw, shoulders, or chest might feel tight, achy, or tender from holding too much stress.

Emotional sensitivity: You may notice yourself crying more easily or feeling unusually fragile in everyday situations.

Headaches: You might experience pressure or pain often triggered by stress, shallow breathing, or unconscious clenching.

Digestive issues: You could have nausea, stomach discomfort, or sudden changes in your appetite that don’t seem to track.

Sleepiness or difficulty sleeping: You may find yourself crashing hard into deep rest or lying awake because you’re unable to settle down.

These symptoms usually fade within a day, although they can last longer depending on the amount of sleep you get, your stress levels, and your overall health. If they’re frequent or overwhelming, though, it may be a sign to get additional support.

The reason panic leaves a hangover comes down to how your body handles stress. A panic attack sends your nervous system into full alert: your heart races, your breath quickens, and your muscles tighten. This is an ancient survival mechanism that’s been designed to keep you safe in an emergency.

The problem? Even when the threat isn’t real, your body still goes through the motions without an outlet to use up that surge of energy.

Once the attack ends, your system shifts into recovery mode. That crash can leave you feeling shaky, sore, and depleted… much like finishing an intense workout. On top of that, the emotional weight of the experience—fear, vulnerability, or the worry it might happen again—can keep your brain buzzing even while your body’s trying to rest.

This combination of physical exhaustion and emotional strain creates the foggy, heavy state that many people call a panic attack hangover.

Related read: Panic attack vs. anxiety attack? Here's the difference

Panic attack hangovers can hit you hard, and you may not have the energy to do much after. These ideas are simple, low-lift, and designed for the days when everything feels like just too much.

Pick what’s doable today and ignore the rest: your nervous system will get the memo.

Your body just ran an internal marathon, and it’s important to be kind to it. If you can, postpone non-urgent tasks and try to give yourself a small recovery window.

Set a 10–15 minute timer, lie down or sit with support behind your back, and let your eyes rest. If you’re at work, try a short break, plus two minutes of slow breathing in a quiet corner. A pause can often help you recover faster.

Related read: Stressed and short on time? Here's how to try micro-meditation

Staying hydrated and keeping your blood sugar steady can help you feel more balanced as your body recovers from a panic attack. Dehydration and dips in blood sugar can make fatigue, headaches, and brain fog worse.

Drink water or an electrolyte beverage and have a simple snack, like fruit with nut butter, yogurt, or toast. This helps give your system some fuel to reset.

Slow, gentle breathing tells your nervous system that you’re safe. Try this for 2–3 minutes: Inhale through your nose for four counts, and then exhale through pursed lips for six or eight.

Longer exhales can help your nervous system shift from fight-or-flight into rest-and-digest mode. But only do this if you feel comfortable. Don’t try to force anything.

💙 If you need some guidance, check out Reset with the Breath with Jay Shetty on the Calm app.

Panic can cause you to tighten your muscles, especially in the jaw, chest, shoulders, and hands. Short, light movements help clear it all without overexertion.

You don’t have to do anything too intense. Simple shoulder rolls, gentle neck circles, a slow doorframe chest stretch, or a five-minute walk around the block or office floor can all help. If you’re seated, simply unclench your jaw, open and close your hands 10 times, or shake out your arms. The point is to loosen everything up.

💙 Need a little extra support? Try the Softening Anxiety Daily Move session with Mel Mah on the Calm app.

Quick temperature shifts, like splashing cool water on your face or holding something cold, can help ground you and interrupt the leftover jitters after a panic attack.

This is because it’s actually a form of grounding that allows your nervous system to anchor itself back to the present moment.

Related read: 18 grounding techniques to help relieve anxiety

Decision fatigue amplifies the brain fog that comes after a panic attack, so try to cut down on the number of choices you’re making.

Trim your to-do list to one or two essentials, and choose “good enough” over perfect. Reheat leftovers instead of cooking, tell your coworkers you’re running a little behind, and move all noncritical tasks to the next day. It sounds simple, but having that space will help more than you know.

Reduce stimulation to ease the post-panic attack stress. Dim overhead lights, switch to warm lamps, lower the volume on any music or background noise, and silence non-urgent notifications on your phone and laptop for an hour.

If noise is unavoidable, try earplugs or a brown-noise playlist. If you enjoy aromatherapy a familiar scent (like lavender, vanilla, or eucalyptus) can also be grounding.

Writing a few lines about your feelings and symptoms post-panic attack can help your brain process what happened and move forward. Research shows that journaling supports emotional regulation, which is why so many people find it useful for panic recovery, too — even if it’s just a quick note or voice memo.

Consider reflecting on what triggered your attack, what symptoms you noticed, what helped calm you down, and what you could do differently next time. This can help give you more effective coping tools for future attacks.

Reaching out, even with a simple text, helps calm the nervous system. Social support is one of the strongest buffers for stress recovery.

Send a text to someone you trust, simply asking to check in. If talking feels like too much, having someone just sit with you can also be helpful.

Related read: How to help someone having a panic attack (and what to avoid)

After a panic attack, your system is more sensitive. Consider skipping or reducing how much caffeine you drink, as it can re-spark jitters. And avoid alcohol, as it’s been known to disrupt sleep and mood. Swap in decaf, herbal tea, or a half-caf and make sure to focus on nutrition and hydration to help support recovery.

Fatigue after a panic attack is real, and quality sleep helps reset your stress response. Keep bedtime predictable with a wind-down routine you enjoy, darken the room, and cool it slightly.

If you desperately need a nap, cap it at 20–30 minutes, and avoid late-evening naps in order to protect nighttime sleep. If your mind spins when it’s time to go to bed, try a quiet meditation or body scan. This can help quiet the mind long enough to help you drift off faster.

💙 Fall asleep with ease thanks to the White Noise soundscape on the Calm app.

Even just knowing what you’ll do next time can take the edge off that heavy, shaky feeling that lingers after a panic attack. One simple idea? Make a three-step plan that you keep on your phone or in your wallet.

Spend two minutes on long exhales or humming.

Splash cold water on your face or run cool water over your wrists.

It also helps to add one contact you trust to call or text.

While you may not be able to prevent every spiral, it always helps to have something in your back pocket (literally) that helps you feel less alone and more ready.

Yes, a hangover can sometimes trigger panic attacks. This is because alcohol disrupts sleep, dehydrates your body, and causes blood sugar swings — and all of these effects can make your nervous system more sensitive the next day.

Alcohol also interferes with the neurotransmitters that regulate your mood, which can amplify feelings of unease or dread. If you’re already prone to anxiety, that extra stress can tip into panic.

Every person who drinks won’t necessarily have a panic attack, but if you notice a pattern between hangovers and panic, it may help to cut back, hydrate more intentionally, or avoid drinking on nights before demanding days.

For most people, the hungover feeling eases within a few hours, but it’s not unusual for fatigue or brain fog to stretch into the next day. The duration of a panic attack hangover depends on several factors: how intense the panic attack was, how long it lasted, how well you slept, and what kind of support you gave your body afterward.

Try to find the recovery plan that works best for you: getting enough water, food, gentle movement, and rest can speed up the reset. However, if you find that your hangover lasts longer than 24 hours or happens every time you panic, it may be a sign that your nervous system is under strain. In this case, getting some professional support can help.

Brain fog and fatigue are your nervous system’s way of asking for recovery time, so supporting your body can make the fog lift faster. Start with water or an electrolyte drink, followed by a small, balanced meal or snack. Light movement like walking or stretching also helps by boosting circulation and clearing leftover stress hormones, while short breaks from screens give your brain a reset.

Some people find that changing environments—stepping outside for fresh air, moving to a quieter space, or dimming harsh lighting—makes a noticeable difference in clarity. Rest is important, too, but you don’t want to overdo it. A short nap capped at 20–30 minutes usually helps more than staying in bed for hours.

The exhaustion you feel after a panic attack is the crash that comes after an adrenaline surge. Basically, when you panic, your body burns through enormous amounts of energy in a short time. Your heart rate rises, your muscles tense, and your brain goes into overdrive to scan for danger.

Even though there isn’t an actual threat, your body doesn’t know that, so it uses up its resources as if there is. Once the panic attack passes, your hormones shift, and your body needs to come down from the emotional intensity. While it’s easy to look at this exhaustion as weakness, it’s really just your body’s way of recovering from an all-systems-on alert. That’s why gentleness is key for recovery.

You can’t always prevent panic attacks, but you can definitely soften the after-effects. The most helpful strategies are proactive, or preventing one before it comes on. Think: getting consistent sleep, eating balanced meals to keep blood sugar steady, staying hydrated, and limiting alcohol or excessive caffeine.

Some people find it useful to have a short aftercare routine ready, too, such as hydrating, stretching, or texting a friend once the panic subsides. This helps to prevent the hangover from stretching out longer than necessary.

Over time, therapy and skills training can also reduce both the frequency of panic attacks and the severity of hangovers. You’ll essentially learn how to give your nervous system a softer landing.

Headaches and sore muscles are common after a panic attack. During panic, your jaw, neck, shoulders, and chest may tighten without you noticing, and fast, shallow breathing could add to the headache.

Unclenching your jaw, rolling your shoulders, or holding a cool compress to your forehead may help. Get care right away if you have a sudden, severe headache, chest pain, numbness or weakness, trouble speaking, or vision changes. If your headache lasts longer than you’d expect, check in with your doctor or primary care provider.

After a panic attack, give your body a few minutes to settle before you do anything else. Stay where you are if it’s safe, and take a few slow breaths with a longer exhale.

Shakiness or fog is a normal part of coming down from panic, so you don’t need to push through it. Once the first wave passes, tell someone you trust what happened and lower the demands on yourself for the rest of the day. The 12 tips above have ideas for the hours that follow. If panic attacks keep happening, talking with a doctor or mental health professional may help.

Mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

#9442. Childhood trauma may leave a lasting “scar” inside brain cells

Severe stress during childhood can increase a person's vulnerability to anxiety, depression, and other mood disorders when new challenges arise later in life. Scientists at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis and Princeton University have now identified a biological process that may help explain how early trauma can have such long-lasting effects on the brain.

Researchers have known that stress during early development can alter gene activity in the brain. The new findings suggest that these changes stem partly from the way brain cells package their DNA. By making certain stress-related genes easier to activate, early adversity may leave the brain more reactive and less able to tolerate future stress.

The study was published Aug. 7 in Neuron.

"We have uncovered a new biological process linking experience of early-life adversity to this long-term vulnerability to mental illness," said Meaghan Creed, PhD, an associate professor of anesthesiology at WashU Medicine and the study's co-corresponding author. "This finding reveals a physical scar left by trauma experienced during development inside brain cells, providing scientists with a concrete biological target to develop new treatments and interventions."

How Childhood Stress Changes DNA Packaging

More than half of children worldwide experience some form of early-life stress, including abuse, violence, or drug use within the household, and other traumatic events. Experiencing four or more of these adverse events is associated with a sharply higher risk of physical and mental health problems later in life.

To understand how these experiences can physically alter the developing brain, the researchers focused on the ventral tegmental area. This brain region contains neurons that produce dopamine, a chemical messenger involved in processing important experiences, including rewards and adversity. When stress causes these neurons to become abnormally active, reward processing can be disrupted, potentially increasing vulnerability to anxiety and depression.

The team then examined the epigenome inside these dopamine-producing neurons. The epigenome consists of molecular tags that help control whether genes are switched on or off, ultimately influencing how cells behave.

Catherine Jensen Peña, PhD, an assistant professor at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute and the study's senior and co-corresponding author, compared DNA inside cells to a coiled slinky. DNA is wrapped around proteins called histones, which help control how tightly or loosely it is packed. When this genetic slinky is tightly compressed, genes are less accessible and remain switched off. When the structure loosens and opens, the genes become easier for the cell to activate.

SETD7 Primes Brain Cells for Future Stress

In young mice exposed to stress, the researchers found elevated levels of an enzyme called SETD7 in dopamine neurons compared with mice raised under typical conditions. SETD7 helps add a chemical marker called H3K4me1 to the DNA packaging system. According to Peña, this tag encourages the genetic structure to open, making the cell more responsive to what is happening in its environment.

To test whether SETD7 itself could produce these changes, the scientists artificially increased the enzyme in young mice that had not experienced early-life stress. As the animals matured, their dopamine-producing brain cells developed a more open DNA structure, making stress response genes easier to activate.

These mice also became less tolerant of stress as adults. Animals that had elevated SETD7 levels when they were young developed more reactive dopamine neurons and showed more anxious behavior than mice whose SETD7 levels remained normal throughout life.

The researchers then tested the opposite approach. After early-life stress, they prevented SETD7 from adding excessive amounts of the H3K4me1 marker. This kept the DNA structure more tightly closed and protected the mice from becoming unusually sensitive to stress later in life.

Even after experiencing stress both early in development and again as adults, mice with reduced SETD7 activity behaved much like unstressed animals. They remained similarly social and exploratory, while activity in their dopamine neurons stayed at normal levels.

The results suggest that SETD7 and the changes it produces in DNA packaging may help create a lasting molecular memory of early adversity. They also give researchers a specific biological pathway to investigate as a possible target for future interventions.

"There are currently no treatments for what early-life stress does to the brain, partially because we have not had a clear picture of what molecular mechanisms to target," Peña said. "This work is exciting because it reveals a clear mechanism, and also helps explain why the impact of stress is both latent and broad. Additionally, if we can step in with supportive care, therapy or social resources to buffer children during those sensitive windows of development, we may be able to protect the epigenome -- preventing the genetic slinky from locking into an open position and perhaps giving the developing brain a chance to build natural resilience."

Materials provided by WashU Medicine. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#9441. The Clearest Sign Of The Winter Blues

Energy, mood or sleep lost to worry? A UK survey found a clearer winter pattern for one of the three.

Energy, mood or sleep lost to worry? A UK survey found a clearer winter pattern for one of the three.

Low energy is the clearest sign of the winter blues among three symptoms studied in young people in the UK, ahead of low mood and losing sleep over worry.

Low mood is also more pronounced in winter, although the difference is smaller.

Shorter days may play a part by shifting the body clock and affecting when young people feel alert, while changes in exercise and social routines could also contribute.

The researchers analysed almost 6,000 interviews with over 4,000 people aged 16 to 24 who took part in the UK’s Understanding Society survey.

They compared interviews conducted in December, January and February with those conducted during the rest of the year, using data from 2022 and 2023 for the main analysis.

On a 0–100 scale, the average score for low energy was about 3 points higher in winter, while the score for low mood was about 2 points higher.

The estimate for sleep lost through worry was smaller and compatible with no seasonal difference.

The figures describe differences between survey reports collected at different times of year, so they give a picture of the group average rather than trace how any one person’s symptoms changed.

Earlier Canadian survey research found that a wider range of depressive symptoms varied by season among young people than among older adults (Lukmanji et al., 2020).

Sleep schedules continue to shift through adolescence and into early adulthood, so the timing of daylight may influence when young people feel most alert.

Winter can also change the shape of an ordinary week, with fewer chances to be active outdoors or spend time with friends in person.

Feeling short of energy could make it harder to stay engaged through a day of lessons or a long shift, even when the person’s mood has barely changed.

The study was published in the journal PLOS ONE (Guan et al., 2026).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9439. Too much or too little sleep may make your body age faster

A new analysis of biological aging across the human body suggests that both sleeping too little and sleeping too much are associated with faster aging in the brain, heart, lungs, immune system, and other organs. These sleep patterns were also linked to a broad range of diseases.

"Previous studies have found that sleep is largely linked to aging and the pathological burden of the brain. Our study goes further and shows that too little and too much sleep are associated with faster aging in nearly every organ, supporting the idea that sleep is important in maintaining organ health within a coordinated brain-body network, including metabolic balance and a healthy immune system," says study leader Junhao Wen, assistant professor of radiology at Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons.

Scientists are increasingly using aging clocks to estimate whether a person is aging biologically faster or slower than their chronological age. These tools rely on machine learning and biological information (e.g., proteins from a minimally invasive blood test) to calculate patterns associated with aging.

Many aging clocks provide a single measure for the entire body. However, different organs can age at different speeds. One familiar example is the decline in ovarian function that contributes to the biological clock associated with female fertility.

Wen and his colleagues have been developing aging clocks that focus on individual organs. The goal is to provide more detailed and potentially more personalized information about a person's health.

"Everyone is excited by these aging clocks and their ability to predict disease and mortality risk," Wen says. "But to me, the more exciting question is, can we link aging clocks to a lifestyle factor that can be modified in time to slow aging?"

Sleep offered researchers an ideal way to explore that question because mounting evidence suggests that sleep plays an important role in health. Wen also had a personal interest in the issue.

"I'm also a light sleeper and was getting worried about the effects on myself," says Wen.

To create the aging clocks, Wen used information from about half a million participants in the UK Biobank. Machine learning was applied to identify biological signatures associated with aging in different organs.

The researchers built clocks using several types of information, including structural measurements from medical imaging, proteins associated with specific organs, and molecules detected in the blood.

"In the liver, for example, we have an aging clock built with protein data, an aging clock of metabolic data, and an aging clock of imaging data," Wen says. "This allows us to see whether sleep is distinctively associated with aging clocks derived from multiple omics and molecular layers."

The team then compared sleep duration (as reported by each Biobank participant) with biological age estimates from 23 aging clocks covering 17 organ systems.

Too Little and Too Much Sleep Linked to Faster Aging

A clear U-shaped pattern appeared across the body. People reporting short sleep (fewer than 6 hours) and long sleep (greater than 8 hours) tended to show faster biological aging.

The lowest levels of aging were seen among people who reported sleeping between 6.4 and 7.8 hours each day.

Importantly, the findings do not show that sleep duration by itself causes organs to age faster or slower. Instead, they suggest that sleeping either too little or too much could be a sign of poorer health throughout the body.

Sleep Duration Tied to Diseases Across the Body

The results also point to a broad connection between sleep, the brain, and the rest of the body.

Short sleep was significantly associated with depressive episodes and anxiety disorders, consistent with earlier research connecting insufficient sleep with mental health problems.

It was also associated with obesity, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, ischemic heart disease, and heart arrhythmias.

Both short and long sleep were linked to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and asthma. They were also associated with several digestive disorders, including gastritis and gastroesophageal reflux disease.

Wen says, "The broad brain-body pattern is important because it tells us that sleep duration is a deeply embedded part of our entire physiology, with far-reaching implications across the body."

The organ-specific aging clocks may also help scientists understand how sleep is connected to individual diseases. Wen and his colleagues explored this possibility by examining late life depression.

The researchers could not establish whether differences in sleep duration caused late life depression or whether depression itself changed how long people slept.

To investigate further, the team used "mediation analysis" to examine whether biological aging might help explain the relationship between short or long sleep and late life depression.

The results suggested that short sleep may be more directly connected with the burden of late-life depression. Long sleep, in contrast, may influence depression through pathways reflected in aging clocks for the brain and adipose tissue.

"This has a strong implication for future sleep management and future therapeutics," Wen says. "Our study suggests there may be different biological pathways between long and short sleepers that lead to the same outcome, late-life depression, and we shouldn't treat them the same way."

Materials provided by Columbia University Irving Medical Center. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#9438. How to write your retirement message or announcement at work

Retirement is the end of an era. And while it’s thrilling to finally have time to do all the things you’ve been meaning to do, leaving behind your coworkers, especially if you’re close, can feel bittersweet.

To bring a sense of closure, many people like to write a message of gratitude to their colleagues before they sign off for the last time. But what do you say? How can you possibly sum up years of collaboration, chaos, and connection in just a few sentences?

Nobody wants the stress of staring at a blinking cursor, so here are a few tips for announcing your retirement and writing a thoughtful goodbye message to the people you’ve worked with. By adapting them to fit your specific role and personality, you can acknowledge the relationships that mattered, offer an authentic goodbye, and leave with intention. Happy retirement!

You might think that your retirement messages need to be a perfect balance of professional, funny, and sweet, but what’s most important is that you sound like yourself.

To ensure that your note is polished and professional, keep these tips in mind.

Most people don’t want to read a long email, no matter who it’s from. A few honest lines work perfectly.

“The time has come. After 12 years of wearing the same pants four out of five days of the week and drinking lukewarm coffee from the break room, I’m retiring. I’ve truly loved working with you and appreciate every wild and wonderful day we shared.”

“Before I officially retire, I wanted to say thank you for this beautiful ride. You’ve all been unforgettable and lovely to me. You’re the reason this job didn’t feel like work.”

“After 18 years, I’ve officially graduated to more peaceful days filled with puzzles and midday naps. Logging off now, grateful for every moment. I will miss you all!”

💙 As you head into retirement, reflect on all the good times you had at work. Gratitude for the Day with Chibs Okereke can help you tap into those positive feelings.

Gratitude makes goodbye messages feel a little warmer. Think about the people or experiences that left a mark, like the coworker who knew your coffee order by heart or the one who always lent you their umbrella when it was raining. (If you need some more guidance, here are eight tips to cultivate an attitude of gratitude.)

“I want to thank my chosen family who made this workplace so special. Your support, humor, and occasional emergency snack stashes got me through some tough days and made the good ones even better.”

“Thanks to everyone who made me feel welcome, challenged, and appreciated. You’re the reason I stayed as long as I did. Well, that, and Barbara’s famous cheesecake. I’ll miss you all (almost as much as I’ll miss all the cake).”

“A heartfelt thank you to my team — you made me better every day. I’m so lucky I got to be a player on this incredible squad. Rooting for all of you always. Can’t wait to hear about all that you accomplish.”

A little story can go a long way. In addition to reminding people of the good times, it can make your message feel more original. You don’t have to write a novel, and it doesn’t need to be profound — just aim for real.

“I’ll never forget the power outage of 2019 when we all played trashcan basketball while waiting for the lights to come back on. We made the best out of a tough situation, and that speaks to the type of amazing people you are. Please stay in touch!”

“Monday mornings just won’t be the same without our doughnut runs. Thanks for the memories, team.”

Let people know all that you’ve learned while working and what you’ll carry forward. Not only will this help fill up your cup, but it can also remind people what they’ve learned while working with you. (Here are 20 questions to help with any potential writer’s block.)

“This job taught me a lot about leadership, teamwork, and that I don’t need to talk louder while I’m on zoom. (Still working on that one…) But most of all, it reminded me how amazing it is to work with such loyal, thoughtful people. I’ll never forget it. Thank you.”

“Beyond the spreadsheets and deadlines, I’m leaving with lifelong friendships, a few more well-earned wrinkles, and countless memories.”

“This place taught me how to lead, how to listen, and how to troubleshoot a broken coffee machine under pressure.”

Some words of encouragement, a simple goodbye, or even a little glimpse of what’s next for you can be a sweet way to sign off.

“I’m off to spend more time traveling, playing with my grandkids, and mastering the art of sourdough once and for all. Wishing you all continued success — and a little less time in meetings.”

“Wishing you all smooth launches, strong coffee, and at least one good laugh a day. Keep crushing it.”

“I’ll be around — probably in sweatpants, gardening gloves, or both. Don’t be a stranger.”

💙 Consider listening to Endings with Tamara Levitt if you’re having a hard time saying goodbye to your work and the people you’ve met there.

It can be tempting to sneak out, but saying farewell to your coworkers is a kind thing to do — and it can help you too. Here’s why:

1. It gives you closure on your terms: Retirement can be a tough transition. One day, you have 50 emails and several meetings, and the next, your inbox is at zero, and you have nothing but time on your hands. Writing a goodbye message can help you mark the transition.

2. It opens the door for real connection: When you write a farewell message, you’re inviting people to respond. What better way to leave than by clearly seeing the impact you had on your coworkers?

3. It lets you shape your own legacy: Your goodbye message can be a tiny chance to shape how people remember you. Go out on a positive note — literally.

💙 Writing to a coworker who’s retiring? These retirement wishes can help you find the right words.

An announcement and a goodbye note do different jobs. The announcement shares your news and your last day. The thank-yous and memories from the tips above can follow it.

Manager first: Tell your manager before anyone else, so the news doesn’t reach them through a group email.

Timing: If you can, send the announcement a few weeks before your last day so people have time to say goodbye.

Subject line: Use a clear one, like “My retirement news.”

Opening lines: Lead with the news, then name who will cover your work.

Long tenure: If you’ve been at the company for decades, add a sentence or two about your time there, and keep the news first.

Here’s an example for someone who’s been at a company for a long time: “I started here 30 years ago, and my last day will be March 31. Over the next few weeks, I’ll be handing off my projects to Marcus and wrapping up my open work. If you’d like to catch up before I go, please grab time on my calendar. I’d love to see as many of you as I can.”

You don’t have to send a retirement message, but it can be one of the simplest ways to wrap up this chapter with a bit of closure and grace. After all, you’ve spent a lot of time with these people over the years.

Writing a short, thoughtful message can help you leave on a kind note. You might also be surprised at how meaningful even a few lines can feel, both for you and the people reading them.

There’s no one right way to send a retirement message. If you want to keep it casual, you could say something like, “After 15 years, I’m off to find out if daytime TV lives up to the hype. Thanks for the talks, laughs, and memories.”

A more heartfelt message you could send is: “It’s been a true honor to work alongside so many talented people. I’m leaving with deep gratitude for my time here — and for all of you.”

If humor’s more your vibe, you could say: “Today’s my last day. Thanks for the memories — and for being so nice about the fact that I was always muted on Zoom. You’d think after a few years, I’d learn my lesson, but I digress. You’re the best, and I’ll miss you.”

Your tone depends on your personality and your workplace culture. If you’re in a very professional environment, a more formal message is the best way to go, but if your usual emails include memes and inside jokes, it’s okay to joke around.

In general, the best retirement messages usually sound like the person writing them, so trust your voice and just be yourself. You’ve earned the right to say goodbye on your terms.

There isn’t a standard checklist, but here are a few good touchpoints that can help you find your flow:

Share a bit about what you’ve learned on the job.

Consider sprinkling in your future plans.

Yes. Email is often preferred in the workplace, as it allows you to reach everyone and provides people with an opportunity to reply.

Whether you send it to your whole team or just a few close coworkers, an email is a low-stress, high-impact way to say farewell. Just remember to hit “send” before IT cuts your access!

If you’re retiring, your thank-you message to colleagues works best when it says who you’re thanking and what they did for you. You can add it to your retirement announcement or send it as a separate note.

For the whole team, a few lines are enough: “Thank you all for the patience and the laughs. Working with this team has been the best part of my job.” For one person, name something specific: “Dana, thank you for answering my questions in my first year. I couldn’t have learned this job without you.” If coworkers gave you a send-off or a gift, a short note afterward can say thanks again.

#9437. Scientists challenge a 70-year-old “lizard brain” myth

Many important choices seem to pit reason against emotion. Popular culture often describes that tension as a contest between two parts of the brain: a newer, more advanced center for rational thought and an ancient "lizard brain" that runs on instinct.

But the evolutionary history of the brain appears to be far more complicated than a simple struggle between old and new.

"There was a theory proposed in the '50s that the brain evolved in layers starting with basic bodily functions, to emotions in the reptilian brain, leading up to sophisticated reasoning in humans," explains Nabil Imam, an assistant professor in the School of Computational Science and Engineering and a faculty member with Georgia Tech's Institute for Neuroscience, Neurotechnology, and Society (INNS). "This is not how an evolutionary biologist would think about the problem."

Research published in Science Advances suggests that brain evolution may be better understood in terms of wiring rather than newer regions being stacked on top of older ones.

By examining the organization of both biological brains and artificial neural networks, Imam and his colleagues found evidence that evolution may involve allocating a limited amount of brain space among competing wiring strategies. Their model describes a computational tug of war between two fundamentally different kinds of neural organization, both of which are established even before birth.

The findings could help explain a long-running puzzle in brain evolution and may also point toward new ways of building AI systems that use less data and energy.

Terms such as "logical brain" and "lizard brain" actually refer to groups of brain regions with very different functions. The neocortex, often associated with higher-level thought, forms the outer layer of the brain and is involved in vision, perception, reasoning, and other complex abilities.

The so-called lizard brain is harder to define so neatly.

"The limbic system, sometimes called the 'reptilian brain,' controls emotion broadly speaking -- but it also has other components with distinct functions," explains Imam. The system contains separate regions involved in memory, smell, navigation, and emotional regulation. "Why do people group all these different regions into one big system? There hasn't been a good theory for what is common between these different circuits."

To explore that question, the researchers compared how these brain systems change across species. Rather than looking at individual regions one at a time, they examined how the limbic system and neocortex vary together over evolutionary history.

A clear pattern emerged. When one part of the limbic system was relatively large, the other limbic regions also tended to be larger. At the same time, the neocortex was generally smaller.

That suggests the regions are not evolving independently.

"Rather," says Imam, "it's a coordinated expansion of these regions across species."

The pattern points to the limbic system behaving more like an integrated network than a collection of unrelated structures. Across evolution, its different components appear to expand and contract together.

The next question was what might cause that coordinated shift.

Imam's explanation centers on the way different brain systems are wired before birth.

Neural circuits in the neocortex are arranged as spatial maps. Brain regions that process nearby parts of the body, such as the thumb and index finger, are also located near one another. Similar spatial organization appears in systems that handle sight and sound.

The limbic system is organized differently. Instead of being laid out spatially, its wiring works more like a bar code, with distributed patterns of activity representing particular smells or complex memories.

The researchers used AI models to test whether these differences arise from built-in architecture or are mainly learned through experience.

When an AI network was created with localized, spatial connections, it was naturally well suited to processing vision, sound, and touch. In contrast, distributed "barcode-style" networks were necessary for strong performance on smell recognition and memory.

An Evolutionary Competition for Brain Space

The researchers then investigated why the relative size of these brain systems changes so consistently among species.

The basic idea is that the brain has limited resources. Space and energy are finite, so natural selection may favor whichever wiring system is most useful for survival in a particular environment.

To test this, the team created a multimodal artificial network in which spatial and distributed systems competed for "real estate."

When the simulated environment rewarded smell, every region within the distributed system expanded while the neocortex became smaller. When vision was favored instead, the pattern reversed.

This trade-off may help explain striking differences between real animals. The nine-banded armadillo, which depends heavily on smell, has a very large limbic system. The squirrel monkey, which relies strongly on vision, has a brain dominated by the neocortex.

Across the 182 species included in the study, the findings suggest that brain evolution is less about adding progressively newer layers of "logic" and more about shifting space between different wiring systems according to what helps an animal survive.

The same principle may have implications beyond biology.

If engineers can reproduce some of this built-in neural organization in artificial intelligence, they may be able to create systems that learn more like biological brains and require far less training data and energy.

"Today's artificial neural networks are trained by vast amounts [of] data -- it's about nurture," says Imam. "But the brain is not a blank slate that gets trained by experience. It is a mix of nature and nurture, and the nature is that pre-wired architecture."

"We could translate that architecture to AI systems to make it more brain-like, or make it learn or function as efficiently as the brain."

This work was a collaboration with Cornell University and was supported by the National Science Foundation.

Materials provided by Georgia Tech. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#9436. What’s Fogging Your Brain? Signs of Aging vs. ADHD

Cognitive changes may stem from perimenopause, ADHD, or early dementia, each of which requires distinct treatment.

Q: How do I know whether hormonal changes related to perimenopause are causing my cognitive function problems, or my ADHD is getting worse, or I might be experiencing mild cognitive impairment or early dementia?

ADHD and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) exhibit clinically different cognitive deficits that help me differentiate one from the other. While ADHD symptoms involve forgetfulness, inattention, and distractibility, MCI has specific cognitive symptoms of word-finding challenges, misspellings, and the use of generic terms like “stuff” and “things” because of word-finding difficulty. Also, MCI is progressive over two to three years, whereas ADHD doesn’t generally worsen.

In perimenopause, a decline in estrogen leads to cognitive difficulties. In contrast to MCI, we know that the cognitive changes from estrogen decline are not the result of neurodegeneration.

However, the specific deficits related to declining estrogen haven’t been well differentiated from those associated with ADHD. So if you have pre-existing ADHD and you experience heightened cognitive difficulties in perimenopause and menopause, you may think, “My ADHD is getting worse.” But it’s likely not worsening ADHD. It’s declining estrogen.

Okay, so what do you do about it? There is a paucity of research for clinical guidance. Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) was not always recommended because it was alleged to increase risk for breast cancer and other illnesses. That claim has now been refuted by the most recent research, which has led to the removal of the black box warning from the FDA on HRT product labels. And so, if I have a female patient with ADHD who is 50 years old and says, “For the past two years, I’ve had cognitive decline,” the question to consider is this: “Do I increase her stimulant medication or do I put her on HRT?”

I am inclined at that point to put her on HRT for three months, keep her stimulant medication dosage stable, and monitor the qualitative changes in her cognitive functioning. If there is improvement on HRT, then the question becomes, “Does she stay on HRT for some extended period of time along with the stimulant medication?” If the HRT doesn’t work or she can’t take HRT for medical reasons, then I might increase the stimulant medication dosage to see if we can’t overcome the perimenopausal changes from the estrogen decline. This advice comes from my clinical experience, and it is unfortunate that we don’t have more research for clinical guidance here.

[Take This Self-Test: Is It Perimenopause or ADHD?]

Q: Could ADHD stimulant medication mask symptoms of mild cognitive impairment?

There is very limited research on stimulants and mild cognitive impairment (MCI). My clinical impression is that stimulants likely improve symptoms of MCI, but do not take that as an endorsement to seek treatment for MCI with stimulants. There is emerging research on MCI and stimulants that has not yet been published. The follow-up question to that is, if you have ADHD and MCI, will treating the ADHD delay the development of MCI or Alzheimer’s? There is no clinical research for me to answer that question. But if this were me, I’d be treating my ADHD, keeping my fingers crossed, and appreciating the fact that the quality of my life on medicine is better than it would be without my ADHD treated.

ADHD should not get worse; however, the experience of ADHD may be worse if life’s demands start to increase and exceed your ability to compensate. However, if you’re having cognitive changes that are beyond the scope of your ADHD, you may have two neurologic processes going on: your ADHD and something else. In this case, your ADHD may, indeed, be getting worse because you have a second neurological process that needs to be evaluated.

David W. Goodman, M.D., is an internationally recognized expert on adult ADHD.

#9435. Q: “My Spouse Complains About My ADHD Constantly!”

“Start with an honest conversation that acknowledges the effects of your ADHD on your partner and explains how it thwarts your efforts to be the best possible spouse .”

Q: “How can I help my husband understand my ADHD so he’s not just complaining all the time about how hard this is for him?”

First, begin by acknowledging the truth of what he is saying: Your ADHD does, indeed, have tangible effects on him. It also has emotional effects; he likely burns much more mental energy than you can see worrying about whether you completed agreed-upon tasks.

Let down your guard for an honest conversation about the impact of your actions (or inaction) on him. Show him that he matters to you and that you empathize with his experience. You may need to spend significant time here; don’t move on until you’re positive that he really feels that you get it.

[Get This Free Download: Manage ADHD’s Impact on Your Relationship]

This sets the stage for the second part of the conversation — how ADHD thwarts your efforts to be the best possible partner. In other words, you have good intentions, even if they aren’t obvious, and you can feel equally frustrated and disappointed by what makes him upset. Also, your ADHD makes your life harder, not just his. While his complaints might be accurate, his too-frequent criticisms are not helping.

Finally, discuss how you can work together to address your hotspots. Ask: What can each of us do, or at least try to do, differently to smooth out some of our pain points? For example, do you want reminders? If so, how and when? Also, does he want to give those reminders?

It’s also helpful to discuss protocols when things don’t go according to plan. How and when can he bring up his concerns in a way that you can hear without getting defensive? How can you tell him that his proposed solution is not working for you?

Encourage your partner to focus on their experience rather than dissecting your actions and making declarations about why you did something.

For example, it’s more effective to say, “It stresses me out when you don’t follow through on commitments because then I feel like I have to take over, and I really don’t want to keep doing that,” versus saying, “You don’t worry about doing things because you know I’ll just do it if you don’t.”

[Download: 5 Ways to Improve Emotional Control at Home]

I often recommend focusing your conversations on what you want in the future, not what happened in the past.

#9434. HEPA air purifiers may boost brain function after just one month

Using an in-home HEPA purifier for one month spurs a small but significant improvement in brain function in adults age 40 and older. That’s the result of a new study we co-authored in the journal Scientific Reports.

HEPA purifiers – HEPA stands for high efficiency particulate air – remove particulate matter from the air. Exposure to particulate matter has been connected to respiratory and cardiovascular illnesses as well as neurological diseases such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s. Environmental health researchers increasingly recommend that people use HEPA air purifiers in their homes to lower their exposure to particulate matter, but few studies have examined whether using them boosts mental function.

We analyzed data from a study of 119 people ages 30 to 74 living in Somerville, Massachusetts. Somerville sits along Interstate 93 and Route 28, two major highways, resulting in relatively high levels of traffic-related air pollution. This makes it an especially good location for testing the health effects of air purifiers.

We randomly assigned participants to one of two groups. One used a HEPA air purifier for one month and then a sham air purifier – which looked and acted like the real thing but did not contain the air-cleaning filter – for one month, with a monthlong break in between. The second group used the real and sham purifiers in reverse order.

After each month, participants took a test that measured different aspects of their mental capacity. The test probed people’s visual memory and motor speed skills by measuring how quickly they could draw lines between sequential numbers, and it tested executive function and mental flexibility by asking them to draw lines between alternating sequential numbers and letters.

We found that participants 40 years and older – about 42% of our sample – on average completed the section testing for mental flexibility and executive function 12% faster after using the HEPA purifier than after using the sham purifier. That was true even when we accounted for factors like differences in the amount of time participants spent indoors, with either filter, as well as how stressful they found the test.

This improvement may seem small, but it is similar to the cognitive benefits that people experience from increasing their daily exercise. While you may not experience a sudden increase in clarity from a 12% boost, preventing cognitive decline is vital for long-term well-being. Even small decreases in cognitive functioning may be associated with a higher risk of death.

Air pollution can negatively affect mental function after just a few hours of exposure. Studies show that air purifiers are effective at reducing particulates, but it’s unclear whether these reductions can prevent cognitive harm from ongoing pollution sources like traffic. Research has been especially lacking in people living near major sources of air pollution, such as highways.

People living near highways or major roadways are exposed to more air pollution and also experience higher rates of air pollution-related diseases. These risks aren’t encountered by all Americans equally: People of color and low-income people are more likely to live near highways or areas with heavy traffic.

Our study shows that HEPA air purifiers may offer meaningful health benefits under these circumstances.

Research shows that air pollution begins to affect cognitive function especially strongly around age 40. These effects may become increasingly prominent as people age.

HEPA air purifiers may therefore be especially beneficial for older adults. Our study did not explore this possibility, as fewer than 10 of our 119 participants were over the age of 60.

Also, our participants only used a HEPA air purifier for one month. It’s possible that longer durations of air purification may sustain or even increase the improvement in cognitive function we observed in our study.

Finally, it is unclear exactly how air purifiers improve cognition. Some studies suggest that exposure to particulate matter reduces the amount of the brain’s white matter, which helps brain cells conduct electrical signals and maintains connections between brain regions. The brain regions most harmed by air pollution are the ones that control mental flexibility and executive function, the same domains in which we saw improvements in our study.

We plan to study whether reducing particulate matter by using air purifiers is indeed protecting the brain’s white matter, and whether it could reverse some cognitive decline. We will explore that possibility by studying how levels of molecules called metabolites, which cells produce as they do their jobs, change in response to breathing polluted air and air cleaned by a HEPA filter.

#9433. Q: “Are My Child’s Tummy Aches a Sign of Stress?”

Here are some patterns to observe to discern whether your child’s stomach pain is associated with anxiety or an underlying medical condition.

Q: “My child has anxiety and often complains of tummy aches. How do I know if the stomachaches are related to anxiety or a medical condition? How do I know when to see a doctor?”

As parents, it’s tricky to untangle common complaints about stomachaches from chronic anxiety, an underlying medical problem, or even school avoidance. Here are a few ways to tell the difference, and clear signs that it’s time to seek medical help.

Understand the mind-body connection. Our gut and brain are in constant conversation. When a child feels overwhelmed, scared, or worried, their body will respond with stomach pain, nausea, constipation or diarrhea, and a generalized discomfort. These symptoms are not imagined or exaggerated; they are physical reactions to emotional stress.

[Download: 5 Ways to Improve Emotional Control at Home]

Observe timing and patterns. When are stomachaches happening? Stomach pain related to anxiety trends to show up during specific times: before and around school, tests, social events, and bedtime. Does your child’s stomachache dissipate after these types of events, or when they are comforted or distracted?

Are your child’s stomach pains taking place at night? Are they making it difficult for your child to eat? Are they losing weight? Is your child experiencing chronic diarrhea or do they have blood in their stool? Are they vomiting? These symptoms are more indicative of an underlying medical condition, especially if they become worse over time.

Keep a log. Track when your child has stomach pains to help you discern whether it’s due to anxiety or an underlying medical condition. Occasional stomachaches that happen during stressful times are common.

However, if your child complains of a stomachache several times each week for more than a month, consult with your pediatrician or seek a gastroenterologist.

[Read: “5 Ways to Reframe Anxiety for Your Worried Teen”]

And remember: You don’t have to choose between taking anxiety seriously and taking physical symptoms seriously. Both deserve attention. By watching for patterns, listening carefully, and seeking help when needed, you’re doing exactly what your child needs: letting them know that any pain they experience matters.

Liz Nissim, Ph.D., is a clinical and school psychologist specializing in parenting and executive function coaching for neurodivergent children and teens.

#9432. Two Everyday Drink Swaps Are Linked To Less Weight Gain

Swapping just three drinks a week was linked to less weight gain over four years. What mattered was which drinks people gave up.

Swapping just three drinks a week was linked to less weight gain over four years. What mattered was which drinks people gave up.

Swapping sugary drinks for water is linked to less weight gain over time, according to a study of more than 140,000 adults.

Replacing them with diet drinks shows much the same pattern.

Switching from diet drinks to water was linked to a much smaller difference in weight.

Both swaps could make a difference by cutting the calories people get from their usual soft drinks.

A diet version can also preserve the familiar sweet taste, which may make the change easier for some people to stick with.

The findings suggest that the drink someone gives up may matter more for their weight than which of these two alternatives they choose.

The researchers drew on three long-running US studies that followed nurses and other health professionals for a typical period of 28 years.

Participants regularly reported what they drank and how much they weighed, allowing researchers to see how their drinking habits and weight shifted over four-year periods.

The researchers estimated about 1.4 kg less weight gain over four years when three sugary drinks a week were replaced with either water or diet drinks.

The estimated difference for replacing three diet drinks a week with water was only about a tenth of a kilogram over the same period.

People who cut back on sugary drinks tended to gain less weight whether or not they increased their intake of diet drinks.

The researchers estimated the swaps from changes in people’s reported habits, so the study can show associations but cannot establish how much weight any individual would gain or lose after making the switch.

Replacing a regular soft drink with its diet version changes the calories while keeping much of the experience of having a sweet drink.

Switching to water also removes the sweet taste, which may change how much sweetness people prefer over time.

In a separate year-long randomised trial, people assigned to replace sugary drinks with unsweetened ones showed a greater drop in their preferred level of sweetness than those assigned to artificially sweetened drinks (Ebbeling et al., 2020).

That change in taste preference offers a possible reason why an unsweetened choice might become more appealing with time.

The study was published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition (Espinosa et al., 2026).
